messages.subject: Major update: Cardinal 2.2 released on Bioconductor 3.9
messages.subject_clean: Major update: Cardinal 2.2 released on Bioconductor 3.9
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Cardinal 2.2 is officially live with Bioconductor 3.9! This is a major update with many changes. Cardinal 2.0 set the groundwork for a migration to the new MSImagingExperiment class, and Cardinal 2.2 fulfills that promise with many new updates, changes, and new features:
Defaults for data import have changed:
Datasets are imported as MSImagingExperiment objects
Spectra from imported datasets are not loaded into memory; they are loaded on-access
All statistical methods (including PCA, PLS, spatial k-means, and spatial shrunken centroids) are now fully supported for MSImagingExperiment
New statistical methods including spatial-DGMM and hypothesis testing via means-summarized linear models and segmentation-based linear models
Pervasive support for parallel computation via BiocParallel
New vignettes documenting both basic use and statistical methods for MSImagingExperiment
Visualization enhancements:
Colorkeys for images are now plotted on the side
Default colorscale for images is now "viridis"
"Dark mode"
Improved simulation of spectra and imaging experiments
Out-of-memory enhancements in matter backend
Exhaustive list of changes documented here <http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/news/Cardinal/NEWS> on Bioconductor NEWS
Please take some time to absorb and get used to all of the changes and new features. A lot has changed in the four short years since Cardinal's original release, and the landscape of MS imaging has changed dramatically.

Just as the original eSet has given way to SummarizedExperiment as Bioconductor responded to the shift from microarrays to next-generation sequencing, so too must Cardinal respond to the evolution toward higher-resolution mass spectrometry imaging experiments.

Some old workflows may break under the new defaults. The older classes and methods will continue to be supported for the time being, but new code should try to use the new world order of MSImagingExperiment.

My sincere hope is that these updates will give us a more robust infrastructure for the future of MS imaging and enable us to more quickly respond to technological improvements while also allowing us to focus more of our time on the development of new statistical methods for MSI.

-Kylie Ariel Bemis

messages.subject: Is baseline correction necessary?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Kylie,

I have a question regarding the MSI data pre-processing pipeline. How necessary is baseline correction and signal smoothing there?
When reading your article  Probabilistic Segmentation of Mass Spectrometry (MS) Images Helps Select Important Ions and Characterize Confidence in the Resulting Segments I came across this passage:

The second dataset (R2) is a mouse brain shown in Fig. 2B. This experiment produced high-quality spectra but with a moderate amount of experimental noise. Mass spectra were acquired on a Thermo Finnigan LTQ linear ion trap mass spectrometer with a DESI ion source over the 200–1,000 m/z range. The images were cropped to remove noninformative spectra. The cropped dataset consisted of 8,950 mass spectra with 9,600 spectral features. The mass spectra were normalized to a common total ion current, and peak picking was performed to further reduce the dataset to 123 peaks. All data processing and analysis were done in Cardinal.

I have two questions regarding this:

1. Is there a universal method to determine if the spectra are high-quality and with a moderate amount of experimental noise?

2. In processing this dataset (R2) you have omitted the step of baseline reduction (as I understood). Is it legitimate to do so?

The reason why I am asking is that when I am doing baseline correction of my dataset, it cuts the peak numbers really violently. Even some ions that have really neat distribution and look nice, are lost after this step ( I have tried various values of the BLOCKS parameter, from 1 to 500). I am looking for species-specific ions in comparison of two datasets, so losing information about these peaks might be really bad. So I don't quite get if I can consider my data high-quality and with low noise levels and skip baseline correction, or missing these steps will make my conclusions invalid? I would be very grateful if you could comment on that.

Best regards,

Olga

messages.subject: Re: Is baseline correction necessary?
messages.body_plain:
1. I am not currently aware of a universally-applicable automated quality control method for raw mass spectra. Some heuristics exist, but I am not sure of any widely-tested and reliable methods. (If anyone has any citations with open algorithms, please let me know!)

Typically, the best way to determine appropriate pre-processing steps is simply visual inspection by plotting the spectra.

2. Baseline correction is not necessary if your spectra exhibit no observable baseline. Some experimental configurations will not produce baselines. In particular, this is not dependent on the noise or quality of the spectra.

s <- simulateSpectrum(baseline=5)
plot(intensity ~ mz, data=s, type='l')

If your spectra do not exhibit a similar trend, and the non-peak intensities are mostly flat across your mass range, then you don't need to do baseline correction.

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: Spatial clustering across multiple samples
messages.body_plain:
The method itself is suitable and does not care what samples/runs a pixel came from; it only looks at the mass spectra/peaks and those of neighboring pixels.

However, it's very common that the run-to-run and/or sample-to-sample variation may be larger than the variation between tissue subtypes, and this can have a major impact on the data analysis

Ideally, normalization would fix this -- and careful pre-processing can help -- but even very good normalization with internal standards can only really do something about the run-to-run variation, and not so much sample-to-sample variation.

messages.subject: Peak align fails
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
i have been trying to investigate why running my PCA-analysis in MSiReader gives me vastly different results to what I get in Cardinal, and I noticed that MSiReader found a lot more peaks. This was caused by the fact that when reading in my data to Cardinal with default parameters, they were binned to only about 3000 bins points, resulting in less than 500 detected peaks. Trying to imrove that, i am now reading in my data with higher resolution (I tried resolution = 0.004 and 0.0005 m/z), and not surprisingly, peakPick finds a lot more peaks, about 75000 (600000 for higher res). However, peakAlign now fails to align them, even though the mean spectrum (which as far as I understand is used to find the reference peaks) looks reasonable. I tried various different values for tolerance and max.diff, but the output data is always just a matrix of 0 (with about 13000 m/z values). Does anybody have some advice on what is the best resolution for reading in the data (in the manual it does say the machine's resolution, which I presume is the sampling rate, in order not to lose too many datapoints) and on what else I could test to figure out where the problem lies? I pasted my code below,
thanks so much,
ilona

data <- readMSIData(rawdata_filename, resolution=0.0005, units="mz", attach.only=TRUE)

dataP1 <- Cardinal::normalize(data, method="tic")

dataP2 <- Cardinal::peakPick(dataP1, method="simple", SNR=3)

plot(dataP2, pixel=1:ncol(dataP2), main = paste("Mean Spectrum"))

dataP3 <- Cardinal::peakAlign(dataP2, method="diff", tolerance=2.5, units="ppm")

messages.subject: Re: Peak align fails
messages.body_plain:
A few things I'll note first:

- The most recent versions of software are R 3.6, Bioconductor 3.9, and Cardinal 2.2
- You're using R 3.5, Bioconductor 3.8, and Cardinal 2.0
- Cardinal 2.2 is a big update, so you may want update when you're able

Apparently peakPick() and peakAlign() for MSImageSet are still using the older Hashmat class to store the peaks; this is a problem here because the m/z values end up being rounded to create the feature names that identify the peaks.

This isn't an issue for the newer MSImagingExperiment class, which uses the actual m/z values to identify the peaks. You can coerce the dataset to an MSImagingExperiment object with as(), or read it in that way when importing:

# read as MSImagingExperiment
myData <- readMSIData("path/to/file.imzML", as="MSImagingExperiment")

# OR coerce to MSImagingExperiment
myDataNew <- as(myDataOld, "MSImagingExperiment")

This class behaves similarly to the old MSImageSet class in most cases, but with better support for higher resolution experiments and some other new features.

The default in Cardinal 2.2 is to use MSImagingExperiment rather than MSImageSet.

Hopefully this would fix the issue.

Also note that the "tolerance" argument is actually for peakAlign() when used on "MSImagingExperiment", so it wasn't being used before (it expects 'diff.max" when used on an "MSImageSet"). This was another part of the problem. Sorry for the confusion during this transition from MSImageSet to MSImagingExperiment workflows...

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: Peak align fails
messages.body_plain:
The code that I posted plots the spectrum that is being processed, with the pre-processing steps applied. The process() function takes a "plot" parameter that will plot the processing performed on each spectrum (if possible). (This is significantly slower than not plotting them, so should be used primarily to identify appropriate processing parameters for a few representative spectra.)

The good news: I was able to reproduce your issue myself and figure out the issue.

A bit of background: peakPick() using method="simple" and method="adaptive" work by dividing the spectrum into some number of regions, calculating the kurtosis (a statistical measure of "peakedness") on each region, and then tries to use the standard deviation of the relatively "flat" portions of the spectrum to estimate the noise.

The problem: The noise was being estimated as NaN, because there were no "flat" portions of the spectrum to use to estimate the noise.

The reason: When binning at a finer resolution, there will be some portions of the spectrum that are "empty", where no data was recorded (because nothing was detected). However, there will typically be a few blips where an intensity was recorded anyway, even if it that intensity is close to 0 (relative to the other intensities). This causes a very "spiky" spectrum in regions that should be flat, where intensities are either 0 or some minimal non-zero intensity. This results in no regions of the spectrum being used to calculate the noise, and the noise is calculated as NaN. This means the SNR's are also calculated as NaN, so no peaks are detected.

The solution: The method is actually working as intended, but there are a few solutions to the underlying issue--

1. Use peakPick(method="mad"). This is the simplest, immediate solution, and should hopefully result in plenty of detected peaks. This tells the algorithm you are mad at it and it must return you usable results, or else. (Joking.) This is a new method in 2.2 that uses the mean-absolute-deviation of successive differences in intensities, and does not rely on detecting "flat" portions of the spectrum, so it should avoid the above issue.

2. Remove the "empty" regions of the spectrum with mzFilter(). This is a new pre-processing method added in 2.2 that (by default) removes mass features with mean intensities below some proportion of the maximum mean intensity. Depending on your chosen bin resolution and how the machine collected the data, it's possible that this will actually leave you with only peaks on its own, and peak detection may not be necessary.

3. Try providing a "blocks=" argument to peakPick(method="simple") with a value larger than 100 (the default). By breaking the spectrum into more regions, the algorithm may find a flat-enough portion to estimate the noise better. I don't recommend this approach, as the noise will likely be under-estimated from regions that almost entirely 0 intensity, but it should work for a sufficiently large value of "blocks".

What I will do: Because the method is technically working as intended, there is nothing for me to "fix". However, keeping a default that may result in no detected peaks for "processed" imzML in a difficult-to-diagnose way is a problem.

In the current release: I will patch the current release to issue a warning and a suggestion to use method="mad" if there are no appropriate regions of the spectrum to accurately estimate the noise using method="simple" and method="adaptive". I will try to do this tomorrow, although it may take a few days after that for the Bioconductor servers to see the update.

In the next release: I will change the default peak-picking method to "mad". I don't want to do this in the middle of a release cycle, but it seems like an appropriate thing to do for the next release if the method is more resilient to issues like this. IME, this method is sometimes too sensitive and has a tendency to estimate noise = 0 in cases like this, but I suppose that's far less of a problem than not detecting peaks at all. Edit: I will also try tweaking method="mad" to have better specificity...

Hopefully the above suggestions will be enough to fix your peak detection issue, and hopefully the peak alignment issue was indeed due to MSImageSet's datedness and hopefully using MSImagingExperiment will fix that once you have peaks.

Thank you for your help isolating this issue (which happens to be completely unrelated to your original issue!) as well as pointing out the typo in the vignette. I will fix that as well.

Let me know if you continue to have issues.

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: Error with MSProcessedImagingExperiment
messages.body_plain:
I apologize for the confusion. The CardinalWorkflows vignettes haven't been updated to reflect the new defaults and changes in Cardinal 2.2 yet.

Using another imaging dataset as a reference is not supported with the new methods, because it is somewhat ambiguous and not totally obvious that it should calculate and use the mean spectrum of that dataset; in addition, the new pre-processing functions use "delayed" execution (see the Cardinal-2-guide vignette section on pre-processing here <http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/Cardinal/inst/doc/Cardinal-2-guide.html#pre-processing>), which means they must store their arguments, which could be problematic when using another (potentially very large) imaging dataset as a reference.

The current way to do what that line of code is attempting to do, would be:

data.peaklist <- peakAlign(data.peaklist, tolerance=200, units="ppm") %>% process()

which will use the means of the detected peaks as the reference.

If you want to follow along with CardinalWorkflows exactly, then you should import your dataset as an "MSImageSet":

data <-readMSIData("file.imzML", as="MSImageSet")

The old workflows using "MSImageSet" will continue to be supported for some time, but the old data structures and methods are not as capable of dealing with high-resolution data as the new "MSImagingExperiment" is.

We are currently working to update the CardinalWorkflows vignettes, but it will take some time. Sorry for the confusion in the meantime.

-Kylie

messages.subject_clean: t-statistics in the topLabels of Spatial Shrunken centroids
messages.body_plain:
Dear Kylie,

I have a question regarding the topLabels output for the Spatial Shrunken Centroids class. It calculates t-statistics, but does it check the normality of the spectrum? As far as I am concerned, the Student test is only valid for normally distributed data.

I have manually checked a couple of features that were assigned to a cluster with a p-value of 0 in my data with a Shapiro-Wilk test and discovered that the feature distribution was not normal (p-val ~10^(-22)), although the Mann-Whitney U test has confirmed this feature as a highly cluster-specific. Still, is it correct to speak of t-statistics if the data is not normally distributed?

The second question, or a remark: in the same topLables output, there is a column with a name "adjusted p values", that as far as I understand refers to the p-value calculated from t-statistics minus the user-set s threshold. Perhaps it might be also useful to have a column with p-values corrected for multiple testing (e.g. Bonferroni correction)? In case of a large output (order of a thousand, for example) this would be very useful.

The third question: I have noticed that in topLables, a feature can be assigned to several clusters with a p-value of 0. Does this happen because when the t-statistics are calculated, the mean intensities in the cluster and in the whole area outside of it are compared? Wouldn't it be more reasonable to compare the mean intensities pairwise between this cluster and all of the other clusters separately?

And the final question: do negative t-statistics values in the topLabels mean that the feature is depleted in the cluster?

Thank you very much for taking the time to reply!
With very best regards,
Olga

messages.subject: Re: t-statistics in the topLabels of Spatial Shrunken centroids
messages.subject_clean: t-statistics in the topLabels of Spatial Shrunken centroids
messages.body_plain:
1. Normality is not checked. In the paper we published about the method (https://www.mcponline.org/content/15/5/1761), we recommend using the t-statistics as a ranking of the relative importance of the mass features in distinguishing different segments. The p-values should not really be considered for a number of reasons. Statistical testing in the presence of regularization is somewhat questionable already.

In newer versions of Cardinal (>=2.2, when applied to an MSImagingExperiment rather than an MSImageSet), the p-values are not calculated at all and only t-statistics are returned (for this reason and others).

We call them t-statistics because they are calculated by dividing a measure of deviation from a mean by a standard error, and they are described that way in the original nearest shrunken centroids paper on which spatial shrunken centroids is inspired. There is no guarantee they actually follow a t-distribution.

Since spatial shrunken centroids is designed for either clustering or classification anyway, it is not truly intended for class comparison or hypothesis testing. The t-statistics are a useful heuristic for ranking the most important features distinguishing each segment, while using regularization to eliminate unimportant ones.

2. The "adjusted p-values" are FDR-adjusted; the given non-adjusted p-values are already from the shrunken t-statistics. Although as mentioned above, newer versions of the method (when applied to the newer MSImagingExperiment class) do not calculate or display p-values at all when they are not appropriate.

3. The t-statistics are calculated based on the differences between the mean spectrum of the segment and the global mean spectrum. They are then regularized (via the "s" parameter) and the mean spectra are themselves shrunken "toward" the global mean spectrum. All of these details are discussed in more depth in the linked paper (which is also cited in the documentation for the method). The t-statistics are used as part of the segmentation itself, rather than a posthoc calculation. They are not intended for pairwise comparisons between segments, but rather being representative of a particular segment as compared to the whole dataset.

4. Yes, negative t-statistics indicate that the mass feature is under-represented in the segment compared to the whole dataset, and positive t-statistics indicate the feature is over-represented in the segment.

* If you are interested in class comparison and statistical testing rather than segmentation/classification, then the newest Cardinal version (2.2) includes new methods for class comparison (see http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/Cardinal/inst/doc/Cardinal-2-stats.html#class-comparison). Note these methods naturally require multiple replicates per condition for statistical validity, so they cannot be used if there are insufficient samples. We don't have a detailed paper or vignette on these methods yet, but we have an upcoming ISMB paper (Guo, D., et al. "Unsupervised segmentation of mass spectrometric ion images characterizes morphology of tissues. ISMB/ECCB 2019) that discusses some aspects of it. We are working on updating the CardinalWorkflows vignettes for our October release.

I hope this is helpful.

-Kylie

Let me also add that a hypothesis testing comparing these classes post-hoc (with a t-test or a Mann-Whitney test or any other test) is not appropriate. This is because in this case the data are used twice: first to determine the classes, and second to test for difference between these classes. The results will be too optimistic (i.e., the p-values will be too small) and not necessarily reproducible.

In contrast, the t-statistics in Cardinal are by-products of class finding. And as Kylie said, their p-values are not necessarily meaningful. Using the t-statistics for ranking only is best.

HTH
OV
